title: Ayudar — the Same Word as Aid

lessons.title: ayudar — "to help", and it is English "aid" in disguise
lessons.gloss: to help — literally the same word as English "aid", arriving by a different road

segments.text: You can ask a question now. The next thing to ask for is a hand — and this verb is one you already own in English without knowing it.
vowel-a — a clean, open a: a-yoo-DAR.
r-tap — one tap at the end, not an English r.
ayudar ("to help") from Latin adiūtāre, the repeating form of adiuvāre: ad- ("toward") + iuvāre ("to help, to delight"). To help was to move toward someone.
English borrowed that identical verb through Old French aidier and calls it aid. So ayudar and aid are not merely cousins — they are the same word by two different roads. The family came with it:
aide, and aide-de-camp, an officer who helps.
adjutant — the officer whose whole job is assisting.
adjuvant — a substance that helps another drug work.

The shape change is a rule, not an accident. Latin -di- before a vowel turned into Spanish y: adiūtāre becomes ayudar, hodiē becomes hoy ("today"), podium becomes poyo. Once you have that, the word stops looking arbitrary.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: a plain -ar verb, and how to ask for a hand

segments.text: Nothing breaks; the endings are the ones you started with:

utterances: person: yo. form: ayudo. meaning: I help.
person: tú. form: ayudas. meaning: you help.
person: nosotros. form: ayudamos. meaning: we help.
person: ellos/ustedes. form: ayudan. meaning: they help.

segments.text: Its noun is la ayuda (fem.), "help" — the word on relief packages worldwide. Two sentences worth owning: ¿Me ayudas? ("will you help me?" — Spanish uses the plain present where English needs will) and, politely, ¿Puedo ayudarle?

segments.source: [YOU SAY: "¿Me ayudas?" — will you help me?]

segments.instruction: "Te pregunto" then "Me ayudas" — I ask you, you help me

segments.text: What two Latin pieces build adiuvāre? (Ad- "toward" + iuvāre "to help".) What everyday English word is ayudar, arriving by French? (Aid.) What sound-law turned adiūtāre into ayudar, and which other word shows it? (Latin -di- became Spanish y; hodiē becomes hoy.) Next: gustar, the verb that runs backwards.
